Make handlers safe during draining, choose how to reject new work, and verify existing requests finish or fail predictably. Persist required background work before exit. Probe intervals and thresholds should fit startup and recovery behavior instead of creating a rapid restart loop.
sections.title: Test the termination path under traffic

readings.takeaway: A health check needs an action model: route traffic, wait for startup, or restart. Graceful shutdown requires explicit ownership, deadlines and a tested drain path.
readings.title: Readiness, liveness and graceful shutdown
wrongAnswers: Liveness, because every dependency failure must restart the Pod
A CPU profile taken once when the image was built

readings.hint: A Deployment revision tracks its workload template.
readings.introduction: A Deployment rollout changes its Pod template and replaces replicas under its update policy. A timeout or unhealthy Pod requires investigation before further mutations. These examples operate only on the inspected development go-api Deployment, using a real tested image reference in place of the placeholder.
readings.nuance: History retention and backward-compatible data changes determine whether rollback can succeed.
readings.objective: Change an image deliberately, observe revisions and understand what rollback cannot restore.
readings.question: What can Deployment rollout undo restore?
readings.reviewAnswer: Restores a retained previous Pod template revision

sections.body: rollout history lists retained Deployment revisions. set image changes the api container image in the Pod template. Use an immutable image digest in a real release where reproducibility matters, and keep the declarative source in sync with this operational change.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout history deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab set image deployment/go-api \
  api=registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.1
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
sections.title: Inspect history and set the intended artifact
sections.walkthrough: Replace the registry, owner and version with a published tested artifact before running. set image mutates the cluster immediately. A future apply from an old manifest can overwrite the change; version-controlled deployment configuration should describe the intended final state.

sections.body: scale changes desired replicas, not the size of an individual process. Check workload state and pressure afterwards. Requests, limits, database pools and worker concurrency multiply across replicas; an autoscaler or another controller may subsequently change the count.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab scale deployment/go-api --replicas=3
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab top pods -l app=go-api
sections.title: Scale with resource and downstream budgets in mind
sections.walkthrough: Three replicas are a syntax example, not a capacity recommendation. top requires a metrics API. Confirm the cluster can schedule the workload and downstream systems can handle its multiplied demand rather than treating replica count as free capacity.

sections.body: undo uses a retained earlier Deployment revision. It can restore the Pod template, but cannot reverse a database migration, external side effect or independently changed Secret/ConfigMap. Inspect the selected history revision and its artifact before a deliberate rollback.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout history deployment/go-api
# After selecting and reviewing an appropriate previous revision:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout undo deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
sections.title: Roll back a Pod template, then verify the service
sections.walkthrough: The undo line chooses the previous retained revision; use --to-revision with an inspected real number for an explicit choice. Afterwards verify readiness, logs and the API through a fresh test request. Do not repeatedly undo merely because a status command timed out.

readings.takeaway: Record the released image, observe the rollout and budget replicas against downstream capacity. Rollback restores a retained workload template, not databases or every separate configuration object.
readings.title: Release operations: rollout, scale and rollback
wrongAnswers: Every database write made by the new version
All deleted Secrets and persistent-volume backups

cautions: A useful automation reduces repeated manual work while keeping changes bounded, observable and recoverable; its command count is not the success criterion.
designGuide.cost: Automation needs explicit ownership, bounded privileges, tests and recovery evidence; a shorter command is not sufficient.
strengths: Connect a service change to tests, delivery, operation and feedback, and choose a small automation project with a measurable outcome.
Make changes reviewable and verify the result against the original contract.

readings.hint: Measure a repeatable outcome and retain failure/recovery evidence.
readings.introduction: A DevOps engineer helps teams deliver and operate changes reliably. Go is useful for portable command-line tools, controllers, exporters and services. The work also involves Linux, networking, release ownership, incident response and collaboration. Start with one service and a repeatable feedback loop rather than collecting tool names.
readings.nuance: A useful automation reduces repeated manual work while keeping changes bounded, observable and recoverable; its command count is not the success criterion.
readings.objective: Connect a service change to tests, delivery, operation and feedback, and choose a small automation project with a measurable outcome.
readings.question: Which sequence forms a DevOps delivery feedback loop?
readings.reviewAnswer: Change → verify → deliver → observe → improve

sections.body: Suppose a Go API must return a new optional JSON field. Write the observable contract and a compatibility test, inspect the current module/toolchain, build one immutable artifact, deploy it to an isolated environment, check a real request and useful telemetry, then promote the same artifact. A green build does not establish that the deployed route reaches the intended version. Record a source revision, artifact digest, target, rollout outcome and a recovery decision. Feedback from production should change the next test or design, rather than disappear into a chat message.
sections.title: Follow one change through the whole loop

sections.body: Before this unit, complete Command line: arguments, exit codes, processes, Git, HTTP and Linux services. Then study Containers and Kubernetes: images, persistent data, contexts, probes and rollouts. The modules lessons explain toolchain pins and build capacity; service-security and SQL lessons cover trust boundaries and transaction ownership. This unit joins those topics into an operational workflow. A disposable local service is enough for the first exercises; paid cloud resources, a public cluster and production credentials are unnecessary.
sections.title: Use the existing foundation in a deliberate order

sections.body: Write down a repeated task, its current frequency, failure modes and time cost. A useful first tool may validate a configuration, produce an inventory report or compare desired and observed state. Give it read-only credentials first. Require a reviewable plan before mutation, bounded work, cancellation, structured output and tests for partial failure. Measure whether the tool reduced repeated manual work without creating a new unowned service. Keep a simple script when it remains clear; move to Go when types, testing, concurrency or distribution make the contract easier to maintain.
sections.title: Choose toil that can be reduced safely

sections.body: These commands belong on a native development machine in a repository you control. Tests need independent assertions; vet and vulnerability checks answer different questions. A clean run cannot prove operational readiness, secrets hygiene or rollback safety.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOMOD GOTOOLCHAIN
go test -count=1 ./...
go vet ./...
go build -trimpath -o ./build/service ./cmd/service
sections.title: Run a local evidence loop
sections.walkthrough: Use the repository’s pinned toolchain and an explicitly reviewed working directory. Do not paste deployment or deletion commands into a production shell while exploring this lesson.

sections.body: Create a small Go HTTP service in a disposable native environment. Define one successful request, a bounded shutdown, a health contract and one expected failure. Write a runbook containing the exact environment, observable symptom, first read-only checks, a reversible mitigation and how to verify recovery. Ask another person to follow it without undocumented credentials or shell history. The deliverable is a working feedback loop with evidence, not a claim to have completed every DevOps discipline.
sections.title: Your first operational contract

sections.body: Return to this capstone after completing the six DevOps readings. Download the complete lab, including independent tests and its README, from https://gopherforge.app/downloads/go-devops-capstone-20261106.zip. The default main.go below uses httptest recorders: it opens no socket and prints readiness 503, then 204, and version 200 with revision local-review. It can be explored in GopherForge. The optional -serve mode listens only on loopback and belongs in a native development environment. Liveness and readiness express different contracts; a successful health request does not prove a successful business operation.
sections.title: Run the capstone model
sections.walkthrough: Run without flags first. newService owns route contracts, demonstrate drives readiness explicitly, and serveOwned owns the native HTTP serving goroutine. On cancellation it clears readiness, bounds HTTP shutdown to two seconds, closes on timeout and joins Serve. Application workers, hijacked connections and deployment traffic draining need their own owners; this example does not establish their shutdown. A revision label, which -revision can override, is not proof of binary identity.

sections.body: In the downloaded lab, run ./verify.sh from a native development machine or a clean CI checkout with a reviewed Go 1.27 toolchain and C compiler for the race detector. The independent tests check response contracts, invalid input, readiness and native cancellation. Retain the generated executable, source manifest, toolchain, build information and executable digest together. Promote those exact bytes after verification; a later rebuild needs its own evidence. Source and artifact digests identify bytes; they are not signatures or trusted provenance attestations. Vulnerability checks, signing policy and deployment decisions remain separate gates.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
export GOTOOLCHAIN=local
mkdir -p build
go version > build/toolchain.txt
go test -race -count=1 ./...
go vet ./...
shasum -a 256 main.go main_test.go go.mod verify.sh > build/sources.sha256
source_id="$(shasum -a 256 build/sources.sha256 | cut -d ' ' -f 1)"
go build -trimpath -ldflags "-X main.buildRevision=$source_id" -o build/service .
shasum -a 256 build/service > build/service.sha256
go version -m build/service > build/buildinfo.txt
printf 'Verified one artifact. Review build/service.sha256 and retain these exact bytes.\n'
sections.title: Retain one verified artifact
sections.walkthrough: The script stops on a failed test, race check, vet or build. It writes evidence into build/, embeds a source-manifest label and hashes the resulting native executable. These shell commands and -race do not run inside the app or browser WASI sandbox. The script performs no deployment.

sections.body: The lab README gives exact commands and expected results. Add an optional service field while retaining the old revision contract: first observe a failing independent test, then fix the code and rerun verification. Demonstrate 503 → 204 → 503 readiness, an unknown route and rejected invalid configuration. Run the native cancellation test under the race detector. Record artifact identity and target, define an SLI event/window, and write a runbook another person can follow: symptom, read-only checks, reversible mitigation and recovery evidence. Describe compatibility and accepted-data handling before choosing rollback. The lab has no database or production load balancer, so it cannot prove data-migration safety, a production rollout or an SLO from a few local requests.

The default model runs in WASI; native server, race-detector and infrastructure exercises require your own disposable native environment. sections.code:
# Go DevOps capstone: prove one service change

Complete the six GopherForge DevOps readings, then return to this lab. The goal is a small, reviewable delivery loop with evidence. Go builds the service and its checks; deployment, monitoring and recovery still need explicit owners.

## Run the local model

Use Go 1.27 with the toolchain version recorded in your evidence. The project has no third-party dependencies. From this directory:

```sh
go run .
```

Expected output:

```text
not ready: 503
ready: 204
version: 200 {"revision":"local-review"}
```

The default mode uses `httptest` recorders and opens no network socket. Copy `main.go` into GopherForge to explore that mode. Listening, process signals, shell commands and the race detector belong in a native development environment, outside the app/browser sandbox.

## Verify and retain one artifact

On a native machine with a supported C compiler for Go's race detector:

```sh
./verify.sh
./build/service
go version -m ./build/service
shasum -a 256 ./build/service
```

The script runs independent contract tests, a race check and `go vet`, records the toolchain and a source manifest, and builds one executable. It embeds the manifest digest in `/version` and records the binary digest. Keep `build/toolchain.txt`, `build/sources.sha256`, `build/buildinfo.txt` and `build/service.sha256` with that exact executable. A source digest is an identifier, not a signature or a trusted build attestation. The `-revision` flag can override the label; the label alone never proves binary identity.

The same `./verify.sh` command can be a CI step after a clean checkout and installation of the reviewed Go/C toolchains. Restrict the job to the permissions it needs. A vulnerability check, provenance/signing policy and deployment approval are separate gates; this script does not establish them.

## Inspect the native service

In one terminal, run the verified artifact on loopback:

```sh
./build/service -serve -addr 127.0.0.1:8080
```

In another terminal:

```sh
curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8080/version
curl --fail --silent --show-error -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz
curl --silent --show-error -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8080/missing
```

Expect the recorded revision, `204`, and `404`. Stop the first terminal with Ctrl-C. The server owner clears readiness, gives HTTP shutdown two seconds, closes on timeout and joins its serving goroutine. It does not own hypothetical application workers or hijacked connections. A real deployment also needs traffic draining and explicit ownership of those resources. The test suite checks readiness transitions directly; this lab does not simulate a production load balancer.

## Acceptance checklist

1. Add an optional `service` field to `/version`. Keep an independent test for the existing `revision` field so older clients remain compatible. Change the test expectation first, observe failure, then implement the field and rerun verification.
2. Demonstrate invalid configuration, an unknown route and readiness changing from `503` to `204` and back. Explain why liveness and readiness are different contracts.
3. Run the native cancellation test under `-race`. Record the process exit and explain which goroutine is joined, the shutdown deadline and what still needs a separate owner.
4. Record the exact verified binary digest and target environment. Promote those bytes; rebuilding for a later environment creates a different artifact that needs new evidence. Never use the `/version` label as a substitute for the artifact digest.
5. Draft a runbook with an observable symptom, first read-only checks, a reversible mitigation and a recovery check. Specify the success/error event and time window you would measure for an SLI; three local requests do not establish an SLO.
6. Write a recovery decision for the optional-field change. Explain compatibility and accepted-data handling. This lab has no database; it cannot prove that rolling back a real data migration preserves writes. Have another person follow the runbook in an environment you control.

Keep a short evidence file with commands, observed outcomes, source and artifact identities, target and remaining limits. A green test run is one input to a release decision. It is not evidence of a production rollout or a complete DevOps qualification.

sections.body: DNS results and routing depend on the actual environment. A successful lookup on a laptop does not establish what a pod resolves. Identify the namespace, search domains, service name, endpoint addresses and caller network policy. Record timestamps and the failing request before changing configuration.
sections.title: Keep the caller in the experiment

sections.body: An address resolving is not proof that the port accepts connections. A connected socket is not proof of the TLS peer name or trusted chain. A TLS handshake is not proof that a route returns the expected version. Use explicit deadlines and correlate a request ID with server evidence. Disabling certificate validation hides the trust failure instead of diagnosing it.
sections.title: Separate layers and preserve identity

sections.body: Write down the expected name, scheme, port, peer identity and HTTP status/body. Change one boundary at a time in an owned disposable environment, re-run the same request, and retain negative cases. Local shell files can model a contract and log analysis, but do not generate DNS, TLS or cluster evidence. The app has no guest sockets, curl, SSH or kubectl; use an isolated native environment for those integration checks.

sections.title: Turn the finding into a regression check
sections.walkthrough: The DNS and TCP observations establish only their own boundaries from the named caller. A TLS hostname mismatch prevents a trusted HTTP request, so no HTTP health conclusion follows. Keep verification enabled, inspect the requested hostname and certificate identity, correct the contract, and repeat the request from the same caller.

readings.takeaway: A useful incident note identifies the first failed boundary and proves recovery from the same caller.
readings.title: Diagnose a service boundary: DNS, transport, TLS and HTTP
wrongAnswers: That the TLS peer identity is trusted and matches the hostname.
That the application route is healthy and returns the intended version.

lessons.explanation: A shell starts in a working directory, and relative paths are resolved there. Before building or moving files, establish that location. These exercises use a new scratch directory on your own Mac or Linux machine; no administrator permissions are needed.
lessons.objective: Use pwd, cd, ls, mkdir, cp and mv in a small disposable workspace.
lessons.title: Bash essentials: navigate, inspect and copy files

lessons.explanation: Most development investigations begin with a filename, a symbol or a short log fragment. Use small commands to narrow the evidence before opening a huge file. The examples assume you are in a trusted Go project and have a text application log named app.log.
lessons.objective: Combine find, grep, head, tail, sort and uniq without hiding their exit behavior.
lessons.title: Find code and inspect logs from the command line

lessons.explanation: Bash is useful for connecting build and deployment tools on a developer machine. Go itself does not require Bash, Docker or Kubernetes. Learning their boundaries helps when a Go program becomes part of a service workflow; these commands are reading examples, not app terminal commands.
lessons.objective: Read a small build script without splitting paths or accidentally invoking a shell through Go.
lessons.title: Bash passes arguments; quoting defines their boundaries

lessons.explanation: A script is another program with success and failure paths. A command printing plausible output can still fail. Pipelines complicate this because the last command can succeed even when an earlier producer failed.
lessons.objective: Read pipeline failure behavior and keep configuration and secrets out of command strings.
lessons.title: Pipelines, exit codes and explicit failure handling

lessons.explanation: A process has a PID, an exit status and open streams. Starting a service in the background does not detach it from responsibility: keep the PID and wait for completion. These commands assume a local Go project with cmd/api and an available port.
lessons.objective: Start one Go service, retain its PID, send TERM and wait for its result.
lessons.title: Processes, signals and exit status

lessons.explanation: A useful script has explicit inputs and predictable cleanup. Bash distinguishes positional arguments, shell variables and exported environment. This lesson puts those pieces into a small test wrapper instead of assuming that adding set -e makes every failure path correct.
lessons.objective: Read required configuration, forward quoted arguments and clean a temporary workspace with a trap.
lessons.title: Small scripts: arguments, environment and cleanup

lessons.explanation: Git records snapshots, not a magic backup of every unsaved editor buffer. Start in an existing local repository and inspect your changes. The sequence below makes a topic branch, stages one reviewed path and records a local commit; publishing comes in the next lesson.
lessons.objective: Keep working tree, staging area and committed history distinct.
lessons.title: Git daily work: inspect, branch, stage and commit

lessons.explanation: A remote-tracking branch is your local record of a remote branch at the last fetch. Fetching updates that record without integrating it into your current branch. The examples assume an origin remote, a main branch and an existing topic branch you own.
lessons.objective: Inspect upstream changes before integration and keep unfinished work recoverable.
lessons.title: Git collaboration: fetch, compare, stash and push

lessons.explanation: A useful Go development loop checks the module boundary, formatting, tests, static diagnostics and the final build. These commands are for the native Go toolchain on a development machine; platform support and build tags can change which packages are selected.
lessons.objective: Use the native Go CLI to inspect a module and check a service before packaging it.
lessons.title: Go toolbelt: modules, tests, vet and build

lessons.explanation: An API can fail before any handler runs, or return an HTTP error over a perfectly healthy connection. curl helps identify that boundary. These examples target your own local Go service at 127.0.0.1:8080 with a /healthz endpoint; adjust the paths to your application.
lessons.objective: Probe a local API and separate DNS, connection, HTTP and application failures.
lessons.title: HTTP debugging: curl, status codes and time budgets

lessons.explanation: A native Go binary can run directly under a service manager; Kubernetes is not required. These examples assume Linux with systemd and a preinstalled go-api.service. They do not apply to macOS launchd or every container environment.
lessons.objective: Inspect a systemd service, follow its logs and understand its restart boundary.
lessons.title: A Go service on Linux: systemctl and journalctl

units.summary: Bash, Git, Go tools, HTTP debugging and Linux service commands.
units.title: Around Go: command line
units.translationNote: Read commands and manifests here; use your own development environment to run them. These tools are useful deployment options, not prerequisites for every Go program.

lessons.explanation: A container image packages a native application and its runtime files. It does not compile Go inside the iOS app, and it does not remove the need to maintain the operating environment. Multi-stage builds let the final image omit the compiler and source tree.
lessons.objective: Separate the build stage from the runtime image and identify what a minimal image leaves out.
lessons.title: Build a small Go image with explicit runtime needs

lessons.explanation: Start with a trusted project containing the Dockerfile from the earlier lesson and a Go service listening on :8080. The following commands use an isolated development container named go-api-dev; an image, a container instance and a published port are different objects.
lessons.objective: Run a named local container and diagnose it with logs, inspect and stats.
lessons.title: Docker daily commands: build, run, inspect and stop

lessons.explanation: Compose defines a local multi-container environment in one file. This example assumes your API reads REDIS_ADDR, listens on :8080 and tolerates transient downstream failures. Use a disposable directory for the exercise and save the file below as compose.yaml.
lessons.objective: Read compose.yaml and use config, up, ps, logs, exec and down.
lessons.title: Compose: run an API and Redis as one local stack

lessons.explanation: A container writable layer usually disappears when its instance is removed. A bind mount maps a host path; a named volume has a lifecycle managed by the container runtime. These local examples use a dedicated fixture and Redis to demonstrate the difference.
lessons.objective: Choose a mount for configuration or persistent state and inspect it without deleting data.
lessons.title: Container storage: bind mounts, volumes and permissions

lessons.explanation: Docker and Podman can build and run OCI-style container images, but their host integration, daemon model, networking and rootless behavior are not identical. An image is an artifact; a container is a running or stopped instance with its own lifecycle.
lessons.objective: Distinguish image, container, host networking and persistent data while comparing local runtimes.
lessons.title: Docker and Podman: images are not running containers

lessons.explanation: A cluster pulls an image from a registry it can reach; a local Docker image does not appear there automatically. Tags are mutable names, while a digest identifies specific image content. Replace the example registry and owner with a namespace where you have permission to publish.
lessons.objective: Tag and push an image you own, inspect its digest and match its platform to the deployment.
lessons.title: Publish an image: tags, digests and target platforms

units.summary: Build, run, inspect and publish with Docker, Compose and Podman.
units.title: Around Go: containers
units.translationNote: Use your own development machine for these command examples. Each lesson distinguishes images, instances, networking and stored data.

lessons.explanation: kubectl reads a kubeconfig and sends requests to its selected cluster as a configured identity. A namespace narrows many workload operations but does not select a cluster. These lessons assume an existing disposable development cluster with a context named dev-cluster; substitute your actual development context.
lessons.objective: Inspect the target cluster and explicitly scope commands before making changes.
lessons.title: kubectl first steps: context, namespace and permissions

lessons.explanation: Kubernetes operates containerized workloads. It does not write your Go code or remove distributed-system failures. A Deployment describes the desired replicated workload; a Service gives selected Pods a stable network abstraction while individual Pods are replaced.
lessons.objective: Read Deployment, Pod labels, resource budgets and a Service without confusing them with an application build.
lessons.title: Kubernetes reconciles a workload; a Service routes to it

lessons.explanation: A manifest declares desired state; the API accepting it is only the start of reconciliation. Save the earlier Deployment and Service example as deployment.yaml, set a real pullable image reference and use the go-lab development namespace from the context lesson.
lessons.objective: Validate a workload document and observe reconciliation rather than assuming apply means ready.
lessons.title: Deploy a manifest: explain, dry-run, diff and apply

lessons.explanation: Read the workload state before changing it. A Deployment, a Pod and a container can each have a different status, so diagnose the layer that is failing. These commands refer to the earlier go-api Deployment in the explicit go-lab development namespace.
lessons.objective: Find the concrete reason behind Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or an unready container.
lessons.title: Debug Pods: get, describe, logs, events and top

lessons.explanation: A Service object can exist while routing to no useful Pods. Diagnose its selector, selected endpoints, target port and application listener separately. This lesson uses the earlier internal Service go-api on port 80 targeting the Go container port 8080.
lessons.objective: Trace a request from a local port through a Service to a ready application endpoint.
lessons.title: Service routing: selectors, endpoints and port-forward

lessons.explanation: Separate application configuration from the image artifact. ConfigMaps hold ordinary configuration; Secrets are intended for sensitive values but are not made confidential merely by base64 encoding. These development examples assume a namespace you own and the permissions to manage its configuration.
lessons.objective: Create a non-secret setting, mount a Secret reference and understand why environment changes need replacement.
lessons.title: Configuration: ConfigMaps, Secrets and update behavior

lessons.explanation: A process being alive does not mean it can accept useful work. Readiness controls whether a Pod receives normal Service traffic. Liveness can trigger a restart. A startup probe can allow initialization before the other probes take effect. Choose each signal according to the failure it should detect.
lessons.objective: Give each health signal one purpose and arrange a bounded stop that drains owned work.
lessons.title: Readiness, liveness and graceful shutdown

lessons.explanation: A Deployment rollout changes its Pod template and replaces replicas under its update policy. A timeout or unhealthy Pod requires investigation before further mutations. These examples operate only on the inspected development go-api Deployment, using a real tested image reference in place of the placeholder.
lessons.objective: Change an image deliberately, observe revisions and understand what rollback cannot restore.
lessons.title: Release operations: rollout, scale and rollback

units.summary: Contexts, deployments, logs, services, configuration, probes and rollbacks.
units.title: Around Go: Kubernetes
units.translationNote: Start with the context lesson and a disposable development cluster. Examples keep cluster and namespace explicit; replace placeholder names and images before use.

lessons.explanation: A DevOps engineer helps teams deliver and operate changes reliably. Go is useful for portable command-line tools, controllers, exporters and services. The work also involves Linux, networking, release ownership, incident response and collaboration. Start with one service and a repeatable feedback loop rather than collecting tool names.
lessons.objective: Connect a service change to tests, delivery, operation and feedback, and choose a small automation project with a measurable outcome.
lessons.title: DevOps is a delivery feedback loop; Go builds its tools

lessons.explanation: A script becomes infrastructure when other programs rely on it. Define its input, output, exit codes and side effects before adding concurrency or cloud APIs. A read-only inventory tool is a useful first project because failure can be tested without changing a real system.
lessons.objective: Design a Go command with bounded input, machine-readable output, explicit exit status and cancellation ownership.
lessons.title: Build a small operational CLI with explicit boundaries

lessons.explanation: A controller repeatedly compares desired state with observed state. Network retries and concurrent operators make “run this command once” an unreliable model. A useful plan says exactly what will change, from which observed version, and what evidence will establish convergence.
lessons.objective: Separate observation, planning and application; use a version precondition and make a repeated successful reconciliation converge.
lessons.title: Reconcile desired state without overwriting a newer observation

lessons.explanation: A source commit, mutable image tag and built binary are different identities. A pipeline can test one artifact and accidentally deploy another. Make every promotion name the exact digest already verified, and keep the build environment and target architecture visible.
lessons.objective: Bind verification evidence and release approval to an immutable artifact, then distinguish application rollout from data recovery.
lessons.title: CI/CD: build once, verify the digest, promote the same artifact

lessons.explanation: An SLI measures a user-relevant outcome; an SLO defines the intended level over a stated window. Error-budget burn relates the observed bad-event fraction to the allowed fraction. It can connect delivery decisions to reliability evidence more usefully than paging on every CPU spike.
lessons.objective: Define eligible events, compute error-budget burn and require both recent and sustained evidence before paging.
lessons.title: Use an SLO to decide when an incident needs attention

lessons.explanation: An incident begins with user impact and uncertainty. A useful responder establishes scope, a current owner and an evidence timeline before trying unrelated commands. Recovery must preserve work the service already acknowledged, including writes accepted after a backup or a server move.
lessons.objective: Use a bounded runbook to gather evidence, choose a reversible mitigation and distinguish binary rollback from restoring persistent data.
lessons.title: Respond to an incident without destroying the accepted writes

lessons.explanation: A green build does not authorize a deployment. Each job needs an identity, a target and a bounded permission set. Keep production credentials out of source, course exports and lab files.
lessons.objective: Separate authentication, authorization and credential lifetime in a delivery workflow.
lessons.title: IAM: give a job one narrow, short-lived identity

lessons.explanation: Declarative infrastructure tools compare configuration, recorded state and an observed provider view. A plan is a proposal at an observation boundary; it is not a guarantee that the world stays unchanged until apply.
lessons.objective: Explain state ownership, review a proposed change and recover from a failed apply without discarding evidence.
lessons.title: Infrastructure as code: plan, lock and inspect drift

lessons.explanation: A request can fail before an HTTP handler runs. Start from the exact caller, hostname, port and scheme, then locate the first failing boundary: name resolution, connection, TLS identity or application contract.
lessons.objective: Collect evidence at the failing boundary without disabling peer verification.
lessons.title: Diagnose a service boundary: DNS, transport, TLS and HTTP

units.summary: Operational CLIs, reconciliation, verified delivery, SLOs, incidents and data-safe recovery.
units.title: Around Go: DevOps and reliability
units.translationNote: Begin with command line, containers and Kubernetes. Go models run locally; real infrastructure, process and monitoring exercises need your own disposable native environment.
